sources.title: Tens of thousands attend Polish nationalist march days afer shootings
Tight security as thousands gather for far-right Polish march

en.title: Thousands Gather for Polish Independence Day March in Warsaw
en.dek: Thousands gathered in Warsaw for the annual Independence Day March on November 11, according to France 24 and The Straits Times.
facts: France 24 reported tens of thousands of attendees, while The Straits Times reported thousands.
The march is held each November 11 to commemorate the end of 123 years of partition by Russia, Prussia, and Austria in 1918.
Poland deployed extra police in Warsaw, and officers installed concrete barriers and searched nearby areas.
Prime Minister Donald Tusk appealed for restraint after ministers said the man who killed six people in Krakow may have been motivated by far-right ideology.
body: Thousands of people gathered in Warsaw on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, for the annual Independence Day March, according to The Straits Times. France 24 reported tens of thousands of Polish nationalist sympathisers at the event, which took place days after a deadly shooting spree in Krakow.

Organizers said they expected a record turnout, with many foreign nationalists including Spain's Revuelta, a youth movement linked to Vox, and members of the Hungarian far-right Mi Hazánk party, according to The Straits Times. Participants describe the gathering, held under the motto 'A Pole is the host in Poland,' as an expression of national pride, according to The Straits Times. Right-wing parties and the now-ruling centrists have long clashed over the march, with centrists saying it is a platform for racism and antisemitism, according to The Straits Times.

Rafal Buca, a spokesperson for the march organisers, said, 'We want a sovereign Poland, independent of foreign capitals ... We also envision a Poland that is as mono-ethnic as possible.' Buca also said that the organisers had condemned political attacks linked to the tragedy, regardless of whether they came from the right or the left. The Straits Times reported that a crowd of thousands gathered under cloudy skies in a central square, many carrying large Polish flags.

Police said they had deployed more officers from outside the capital in Warsaw, declining to give numbers, according to The Straits Times. Concrete barriers were installed on streets adjacent to the starting point downtown, while officers searched nearby areas, according to The Straits Times. Authorities have in the past attempted to stop the march following clashes between some participants and their political opponents or police, according to The Straits Times.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in Szczecin, northwestern Poland, that anyone who truly cares about Poland must understand that the space defined by independence, freedom, and a secure Republic is a common good. The Straits Times reported that Tusk appealed for restraint amid sharper-than-usual political divisions after ministers outraged nationalists by saying the man who killed six people in the main square of Krakow may have been motivated by far-right ideology.
en.context: The event is held each November 11 to commemorate the ending in 1918 of 123 years of partition by Russia, Prussia and Austria, according to France 24. France 24 reported that while the march has generally been peaceful, some rallies in the past have been marred by clashes with police or counter-demonstrators.

problemsFixed: Sources disagree on crowd size: France 24 reported tens of thousands, while The Straits Times reported thousands; the draft presents both figures without noting the discrepancy.
Every body paragraph contains only one sentence; the style guide requires 2-4 sentences per paragraph.

The draft omits concrete details present in the sources: the six people killed in Krakow, ministers' claim about far-right ideology, the march motto, past attempts by authorities to stop the event, and security measures such as concrete barriers.
The dek and title use contested labels ('far-right', 'nationalist') without attribution.
Several claims lack direct attribution, including the installation of concrete barriers and past clashes.
